messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 54
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Civil Servant
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by romantic partner
  pcl5: 59

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Loss of Control: Lack of control, Sleeping Alone: Sleeping alone or in an unfamiliar place, Male Presence: Being alone with men
  Maladaptive Strategies: Memory Detachment: I detach myself from the memories, Constant Socialising: I keep myself constantly surrounded by people so I am never alone with my thoughts, Avoid Being Alone: Being alone in a room or building
  Memory: Hard to Recall Deliberately: When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory, Taste Vividness: I can taste what I tasted during the event when the memory returns, Photographic Recall: Remembering what happened during the frightening event is just like looking at photographs of it in my mind.

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Daniel was 54 and worked as a civil servant in a role that kept him in and out of municipal offices, meeting rooms, and public buildings throughout the week. By the time he came for help, he was living with a persistent sense that certain ordinary situations could suddenly become dangerous in the same way they had when he was being physically abused by a former romantic partner years earlier. He did not speak about that relationship easily. When he first tried to describe what had happened, he often stopped, looked away, and said that the details were “hard to get hold of.” He could not deliberately summon the memory in a smooth, continuous way; instead, it came in fragments, as if he were trying to access something sealed behind glass.

What Daniel could remember, however, was sharply sensory and exact when it surfaced. He described those moments as if he were looking at a series of photographs in his mind, each one frozen and separate. He could recall the room, the position of the furniture, the angle of his own body, and the instant his partner’s expression changed before the abuse began. Alongside those images came a taste he found impossible to ignore, a vivid metallic or bitter sensation that returned with the memory and made him feel briefly as though he were back in that period. He said it was not like telling a story from the past; it was more like being hit by a picture and a taste at the same time, with no transition in between. Even now, when a memory came unexpectedly, the scene felt startlingly visual and concrete, but not easy for him to put into words on purpose.

In the years after the relationship ended, Daniel gradually reorganized his life around keeping those moments at a distance. He said he detached himself from the memories whenever possible, not because they were absent, but because if he let himself dwell on them he became preoccupied with the sense that the past was still too close. He kept himself constantly surrounded by people so he was never alone with his thoughts. After work he arranged dinners, long phone calls, social visits, and errands that would keep him moving from one person to another. Even at home, he preferred background noise and open doors. Being alone in a room or building unsettled him, and he would leave lights on or go out to sit in a café rather than stay by himself in silence. He described these habits not as choices that felt especially helpful, but as the only way he could tolerate an evening without becoming absorbed in what had happened.

Certain situations carried the force of that past more than others. What frightened him most was a loss of control. He found himself tense in moments when he could not easily predict what would happen next or when he felt trapped by another person’s decision. In meetings at work, if a discussion became heated and he felt he had little say, he noticed the familiar tightening in his body and an urge to get away. He was also wary of sleeping alone or staying overnight in an unfamiliar place. On business trips for his civil service job, he often accepted extra social plans simply so he would not have to return to a hotel room by himself, and if that could not be avoided, he slept poorly and stayed alert to every sound. Being alone with men was another trigger that had become especially difficult for him. He managed this by adjusting his routines so that he was rarely in one-on-one situations with male colleagues, tradesmen, or neighbors, and he felt safer when there were other people nearby. These arrangements shaped his days in practical ways and sometimes made him seem more available than he wanted to be, because he would rather join a group than risk a quiet setting with only one man present.

Daniel was in a relationship now, but he had not fully disclosed how much he organized his life around not being alone. His partner had noticed that he was always trying to fill the calendar and that he became uneasy when plans fell through and he had to sit with himself. At work, he remained competent and reliable, though he had started avoiding certain assignments that required overnight stays or prolonged solitary time in unfamiliar settings. The strain of maintaining these patterns had become harder to hide, especially as he aged and found he had less energy for constantly keeping himself occupied. He sought therapy after a stretch in which he found himself increasingly unsettled by being by himself at home and increasingly aware that his usual ways of managing were limiting both his work and his relationship. He came hoping to understand why those specific situations — being alone, being without control, and being alone with men — still felt so charged, and he was most afraid that if he stopped surrounding himself with others, the memories would come back with the same vividness and force they had before.
